topics: ⏳ What Exactly Is 'A Period of Fitness'? — Ḥizkiya (slaughter) vs. Rabbi Yoḥanan (eating), with 'sprinkling' floated as a third reading
🌙 The 'Overnight' Case Re-examined — was it the blood or the meat that remained overnight, and what does that prove?
🚫 Blood Collected by an Unfit Priest — does that alone create me'ilah, or only if he also sprinkles it?
🧺 Rendering Blood 'Leftovers' — Reish Lakish asks Rabbi Yoḥanan which invalid sprinklings turn remaining blood into shirayim
🔁 One More Round on 'The Piggul Is Always Subject to Me'ilah' — testing whether it proves the sprinkling-reading or supports Rav Giddel

overview.title: 📖 Overview: Pinpointing 'A Period of Fitness'
overview.subtitle: Meilah 5a–5b
overview.hebrewSource: לָא דַּיְיקָא מַתְנִיתִין דְּלָא כְּחִזְקִיָּה וּדְלָא כְּרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: Building on bar Kappara's question from the end of the last daf, the Gemara records the actual dispute: Ḥizkiya says Rabbi Yehoshua's 'period of fitness for the priests' means fitness of slaughtering, while Rabbi Yoḥanan says it means fitness of actually eating the offering's meat. Rabbi Zeira observes that a careful reading of the mishna fits neither view precisely, and the Gemara spends the daf testing the mishna's cases — the overnight case, blood collected or sprinkled by unfit priests — against a third possibility: fitness of sprinkling. Along the way Rav Asi, Rav Yosef, and a related dispute between Reish Lakish and Rabbi Yoḥanan about when an invalid sprinkling renders the remaining blood 'leftovers' all get folded into the analysis, which circles back to confirm Rav Giddel's rule about piggul and me'ilah.

slides.title: ⏳ Three Candidate Readings of 'A Period of Fitness'
slides.subtitle: When exactly does an offering stop being subject to me'ilah?

boxes.title: Ḥizkiya: Fitness of Slaughter
items: Once properly slaughtered, later disqualification does not bring back me'ilah

boxes.title: Fitness of Sprinkling (floated)
items: Once the blood is ready/fit to be sprinkled — even if not yet actually sprinkled
A middle position tested throughout the daf

boxes.title: Rabbi Yoḥanan: Fitness of Eating
items: Only once the blood was actually, properly sprinkled and the meat became permitted to priests

callout.label: Rabbi Zeira's observation:
callout.text: A precise reading of the mishna's own cases doesn't line up cleanly with either Ḥizkiya's or Rabbi Yoḥanan's position — prompting the Gemara to test the 'sprinkling' reading against the text.

slides.title: 🌙 Did the Blood or the Meat Remain Overnight?
slides.subtitle: Testing the mishna's 'notar' case for a hidden proof

nodes.content: ❓ Mishna: an offering 'that remained overnight' had a period of fitness — no me'ilah. Does 'remained overnight' mean the blood, still unsprinkled?
💡 If so: slaughter + collection were proper, but sprinkling never happened — yet still no me'ilah!
📊 That would prove: fitness of SPRINKLING is what Rabbi Yehoshua meant — against both Ḥizkiya and Rabbi Yoḥanan
🔄 Gemara rejects this: the case means the MEAT remained overnight — the blood was already properly sprinkled
✅ So this case actually supports Rabbi Yoḥanan: fitness of EATING (sprinkling was completed, meat was permitted, then it became notar)

callout.label: Round one:
callout.text: The attempted proof for 'fitness of sprinkling' fails — the overnight case is reinterpreted to fit Rabbi Yoḥanan instead.

slides.title: 🚫 Collected by an Unfit Priest, Sprinkled by a Fit One?
slides.subtitle: A second attempt to prove 'fitness of sprinkling', tested against a parallel mishna in Zevaḥim
rows: 'Collected and sprinkled by unfit priests' must mean collected by unfit, sprinkled by fit (else why mention both?)
Suggests: if collected by FIT priests, blood is already 'fit for sprinkling' — no me'ilah even before actual sprinkling
A parallel mishna (Zevaḥim 92a) about a sin offering's blood requiring laundering uses the same 'collected/sprinkled by unfit' language
If read the same way, it wrongly implies blood collected by a fit priest but sprinkled by an unfit one requires laundering — but the verse (Lev. 6:20) excludes any already-sprinkled blood
Maybe the Zevaḥim mishna is simply imprecise (לָאו דַּוְקָא) in its wording
Rav Asi objects: then why would BOTH mishnayot use identical imprecise language? At least one must be exact
The Meilah mishna is the precise one; the Zevaḥim mishna is the imprecise one
Confirms: 'fitness of sprinkling' IS the correct reading of Rabbi Yehoshua's principle — and the Zevaḥim mishna instead teaches that an unfit priest's collection renders blood 'leftovers' (שירים)

lines.speaker: Reish Lakish
lines.text: If an unfit priest sprinkles some of the blood, does that render the remaining blood 'leftovers' (שירים), so a later valid sprinkling accomplishes nothing?

lines.speaker: R' Yoḥanan
lines.text: Only a sprinkling done with piggul intent — chutz lizmano or chutz limkomo — creates leftovers, since such a sprinkling still 'accepts' the offering for piggul purposes.

lines.speaker: Gemara asks
lines.text: Does that exclude every other unfit sprinkling, including one by a ritually impure priest?

lines.speaker: Clarified
lines.text: No — an impure priest IS included, since impurity does not disqualify him from serving when most of the community is impure (offerings of the community override tumah). Only sprinklings that could NEVER count for the community — like a blemished priest's — fail to create leftovers.

callout.label: Net result:
callout.text: Piggul-intent sprinklings and an impure priest's sprinkling both render remaining blood 'leftovers'; other invalid sprinklings (e.g., by a blemished priest) do not.

slides.title: 🔁 Back to 'The Piggul Is Always Subject to Me'ilah'
slides.subtitle: A final test — and confirmation of Rav Giddel's rule
slides.hebrewSource: זְרִיקַת פִּיגּוּל – אֵינוֹ מוֹצִיא מִידֵי מְעִילָה, וְאֵינוֹ מֵבִיא לִידֵי מְעִילָה
slides.label: The last round:
slides.text: The Gemara reconsiders the baraita 'a piggul offering is always subject to me'ilah.' If it refers to blood collected but not yet sprinkled, it would support 'fitness of sprinkling.' But the Gemara instead reads it as referring to blood already sprinkled with piggul intent — meaning even after sprinkling, sacred-order piggul offerings remain subject to me'ilah. The word 'always' (לְעוֹלָם) is there specifically to teach Rav Giddel's rule: piggul sprinkling neither removes sacred-order offerings from me'ilah nor brings offerings of lesser sanctity into it.

summary.principle: Rabbi Yehoshua's 'period of fitness for the priests' is tested through the mishna's own cases and parallel sources; the Gemara ultimately reads it as fitness of sprinkling, while separately confirming Rav Giddel's rule that a piggul-intent sprinkling neither exempts sacred-order offerings from me'ilah nor creates me'ilah for offerings of lesser sanctity.

flowSteps.content: ⏳ Three candidate readings: fitness of slaughter (Ḥizkiya), of sprinkling, or of eating (R' Yoḥanan)
🌙 'Overnight' case reinterpreted: the MEAT remained overnight after valid sprinkling — supports 'eating'

columns.content: 🚫 'Collected by unfit, sprinkled by fit' case, refined via the Zevaḥim parallel, ultimately supports 'sprinkling'
🧺 Piggul-intent (and impure-priest) sprinklings render remaining blood 'leftovers'; others do not

flowSteps.content: 🔁 'The piggul is always subject to me'ilah' — read as after sprinkling, confirming Rav Giddel
🎓 Key Principle: 'A period of fitness' = fitness of sprinkling; piggul sprinkling itself never removes or creates me'ilah

quiz.q: What do Ḥizkiya and Rabbi Yoḥanan each say Rabbi Yehoshua meant by 'a period of fitness for the priests'?
o: Ḥizkiya: fitness of eating; Rabbi Yoḥanan: fitness of slaughtering
Ḥizkiya: fitness of slaughtering; Rabbi Yoḥanan: fitness of eating the meat
Both agree it means fitness of sprinkling
Ḥizkiya: fitness of sprinkling; Rabbi Yoḥanan: fitness of slaughtering
quiz.e: Ḥizkiya holds that a properly performed slaughter alone starts the 'period of fitness'; Rabbi Yoḥanan holds it requires that the meat actually became permitted for priestly consumption.

quiz.q: How does the Gemara ultimately explain the mishna's case of an offering 'that remained overnight' (notar)?
o: The blood remained overnight, unsprinkled
The meat remained overnight, after the blood had already been properly sprinkled
Both the blood and the meat remained overnight
The mishna is not discussing notar at all
quiz.e: The Gemara rejects reading it as unsprinkled blood and instead explains it as meat left overnight after valid sprinkling — supporting Rabbi Yoḥanan's 'fitness of eating' reading in that round.

quiz.q: Why does Rav Asi object to saying that the Zevaḥim mishna about a sin offering's blood is simply worded imprecisely (לאו דווקא)?
o: Because imprecise wording is never used in the Mishna
Because if that mishna is imprecise, and our Meilah mishna uses the same style, we'd have no reason to think either is precise — but the Meilah mishna should be exact
Because sin offerings are never discussed imprecisely
Because the verse in Leviticus contradicts the mishna entirely
quiz.e: Rav Asi reasons that since both mishnayot use identical phrasing, it's implausible that both are imprecise; the conclusion is that the Meilah mishna is precise and the Zevaḥim one is not.

quiz.q: According to Rabbi Yoḥanan's answer to Reish Lakish, which invalid sprinkling(s) render the remaining blood 'leftovers' (shirayim)?
o: Any sprinkling by any unfit priest, without exception
Only sprinkling done with piggul intent (and, as clarified, sprinkling by an impure priest in communal offerings)
No invalid sprinkling ever creates leftovers
Only sprinkling performed by a blemished priest
quiz.e: Rabbi Yoḥanan limits this to piggul-intent sprinklings (which still 'accept' the offering) and, as the Gemara clarifies, an impure priest serving when tumah is overridden for the community — but not other invalid sprinklers like a blemished priest.

quiz.q: How does the Gemara's final analysis of 'the piggul is always subject to me'ilah' connect to Rav Giddel's teaching?
o: It contradicts Rav Giddel and proves 'fitness of sprinkling' instead
It is read as referring to blood already sprinkled with piggul intent, confirming that sprinkling with piggul intent does not remove sacred-order offerings from me'ilah
It proves that piggul offerings are never subject to me'ilah
It has no connection to Rav Giddel's teaching
quiz.e: The baraita's word 'always' is understood to mean that even after a piggul-intent sprinkling, offerings of the most sacred order remain subject to me'ilah — exactly Rav Giddel's rule.
